newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-THE OLD WAYS ARE BEST FOR SKAARDAL.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-THE OLD WAYS ARE BEST FOR SKAARDAL.

text.p: Some sayings seem tailor-made for Atle Skaardal.
"You can't teach an old dog new tricks" and "if it ain't broke don't fix it" spring to mind.

After the 30-year-old Norwegian won the opening race of the Alpine skiing world championships on Monday to retain the super-giant slalom title, he was asked whether changes to his team structure had been important.
The Norwegian men's team have a new German coach this season who has introduced some new techniques.
Skaardal said it was all the same really.
"I'm too old to learn new things now," he told a news conference after beating younger compatriot Lasse Kjus into second place. "I just have to do what I can."
Skaardal, who has been on the men's World Cup circuit since 1984 but won his first major medal only in 1993, has taken his time to get to the top.
"I had my first race in 1984 and it was a very long time ago," he said. "I think you need to be around for a while to get your confidence.
"In my early years I had so much respect for skiers like Pirmin Zurbriggen and Helmut Hoeflehner. Then (Norway's) Ole-Christian Furuseth showed the way and the whole team came after him," he said.
Furuseth won his first World Cup race in 1989 and Skaardal triumphed the following year for the first time. He then captured a downhill silver at the 1993 championships.
Having found the path to success and climbed to the top of the hill in Sierra Nevada, southern Spain, in 1996, Skaardal just did what he could and hoped for the best.
"Today I was very relaxed," he said.
"I was thinking about the gold from last year and that it doesn't really matter how it goes today."
Skaardal was the fifth starter on the Kandahar-Banchetta piste and was followed down by Kjus.
Kjus later jokingly portrayed his venerable older team mate as more of a wily old fox.
"Atle told me there were some really difficult turns down there and to slow down the speed a little bit," he said. "I think that's where he won the race."
"He said something about some FIS (International Ski Federation) guys standing below the jumps and to go to the left to avoid them," he added with a smile.
At the Sierra Nevada championships, Russian women's downhiller Tatiana Lebedeva came over a rise during training and hit an FIS official on the piste.
Skaardal's win was a surprise but so was Kjus's silver in a season that has seen him sidelined by illness after capturing the overall World Cup crown last year.
"There was a time when I thought I would never be well again, I felt so bad," he said.

"Before this race I thought that I had a small chance to reach the podium. When I came into the finish, I was hoping to see my name in the top six. I checked at the bottom and thought 'oh, this was a bad one'. Then I looked up."
Kjus, who faces an operation on his sinuses over the summer, felt he had a good chance in other races but would not compete in the slalom at the end of the final week.
"This year I want to try the night life at the championships," he said. "I haven't had a chance before."
